newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia minister calls for recognition of rebels.
newsitem.headline: Colombia minister calls for recognition of rebels.

text.p: Colombia's leftist guerrilla armies should be recognised as "belligerent forces" and accorded political status, Interior Minister Horacio Serpa said on Tuesday amid growing demands for a new peace process to end the country's long-running conflict.

The comments were a significant departure from the traditional tactic of dubbing rebel groups "narco-terrorists" and "bandits." If the suggestions are adopted as government policy it could open the way to a dialogue with rebel forces.

Recognising the rebels as "belligerent forces" could also open the way for them to receive wider international recognition as legtimate combatants, a move the government has fiercely resisted until now.

Serpa, seen as Samper's right-hand man, commented after new Defence Minister Gilberto Echeverri proposed starting peace talks with Marxist rebels and right-wing paramilitaries in a bid to end Colombia's three-decade-old uprising.

"The guerrilla is a power, uncomfortable, illegal, criminal or whatever else you want to call it. But we must recognise that it is a belligerent, pressure force," Serpa told Colombia's leading El Tiempo newspaper.
"Moreover, however uncomfortable it may be ... to sit down and talk with the guerrilla we must recognise it has a political aspect," he added.

No formal peace proposal has been drafted but Echeverri said he would look to set up state institutions that would carry on negotiations irrespective of the government in power. He said talks should include representatives of government, business, grassroots organisations and the church as well as military, rebel and paramilitary leaders.

The response from the armed groups involved in the conflict has been muted. Two paramilitary forces have said they would be willing to talk peace but the main guerrilla armies, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), set up as a pro-Soviet force in 1964, and the National Liberation Army (ELN), founded by radical Roman Catholic priests in the mid-1960s, have not yet publicly responded.

Previous peace deals at the end of the 1980s led to the majority of the leftist M-19 and the Maoist-inspired People's Liberation Army (EPL) laying down their arms. But so far efforts to strike an accord with the FARC and ELN have failed.
